panels.rationale: Single clinical photo of perioral/lip area captioned 'Chronic skin lesions of EPP' in EPP review; in-text describes waxy leathery thickening and characteristic lip linear furrows/pseudo-rhagades, both visible.
panels.attribution_text: Lecha et al. Erythropoietic protoporphyria.. Orphanet journal of rare diseases 2009. doi:10.1186/1750-1172-4-19. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
in_text_mentions: in altered skin appearance with permanent changes, such as skin thickening with a waxy or leathery appearance, and areas of hyperkeratosis. These lesions are usually located on the dorsa of the hands and face, as these are skin areas usually exposed (Fig. 4). The lips show linear furrows and pseudo-rhagades that arte also characteristic. In contrast to other forms of cutaneous porphyria, lesions of milia, hypertrichosis or hyperpigmentation do not appear. This last cutaneous sign may only appear in patients with severe hepatic involvement presenting with cholestasis, itching and jaundice [2].

in_text_mentions: Cutaneous lesions result from the presence of protoporphyrin in erythrocytes and plasma in skin vasculature. Histologically, hyaline PAS-positive perivascular material deposits can be found together with extensive presence of fine fibrillar material, and reduplication of blood vessel walls and epidermal basal lamina. Although less prominent, these findings appear also in other cutaneous porphyrias (Fig 5).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Clinical photo of EPP patient per article title and caption describing flaky skin with blood crusts on lips/mouth; no vocabulary finding matches so captured as proposed findings. B: Clinical photo of same EPP patient showing slightly thickened skin on finger joints matching waxy lichenified thickening vocabulary, plus blood crust lesions. C: Gross photo of liver biopsy tissue strips from EPP patient; dark pigmentation visible, related to hepatic protoporphyrin deposition shown in panel D, no vocabulary finding so proposed. D: H&E liver histopathology from EPP patient explicitly described with Maltese-cross birefringent pigment in Kupffer cells, matching vocabulary. E: Immunofluorescence of erythrocytes from EPP patient showing fluorescent protoporphyrin-loaded erythrocytes, matching birefringent erythrocytes synonym of Maltese-cross finding.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: H&E liver-biopsy panel from the EPP re-biopsy described in an EPP-definitive article; it visibly contains brown hepatic deposits consistent with protoporphyrin accumulation, but the polarization evidence is in panel b, so attribution is slightly less direct for this panel alone. b: Polarized-light histology of the EPP re-biopsy shows reddish polarized material at the periphery of brown hepatic deposits, supporting protoporphyrin/Maltese-cross-type birefringence in a real patient liver specimen from an EPP-confirmed case.
panels.attribution_text: Miyakami et al. Definitive Confirmation of Erythropoietic Protoporphyria via Re-biopsy Three Years After Initial Liver Biopsy at Age 15.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.38017. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Polarized light observation of the re-biopsy specimen a: Hematoxylin and eosin stain. b: Under observation by polarized light, reddish-colored materials are seen at the periphery of the brown deposits (arrow).
in_text_mentions: ytic infiltration and fibrosis were seen in the portal area. The degree of fibrosis was more prominent than in the first liver biopsy and fibrous septa extended from the portal area, showing bridging fibrosis in places. Dark brown to light brown deposits were observed at the margins of the fibrous septa and within the liver parenchyma. Some of these were located in the sinusoids, mainly inside Kupffer cells (Figure 2). Iron stain and copper stain (use orcein stain) were not found. Some of the brown deposits showed weak polarization and a reddish color in polarized light observation (Figure 3).

A: H&E liver biopsy from the EPP case report showing nodular hepatocellular hyperplasia with fibrous septa and bile duct proliferation (black arrows), described in the article as part of the hepatic pathology of erythropoietic protoporphyria. Human patient tissue; findings are named but absent from the provided vocabulary, so they are listed as proposed findings. B: H&E liver biopsy (40×) from the EPP patient showing hepatocellular steatosis and dense brown granular protoporphyrin deposits within hepatic sinusoids and hepatocytes (black arrow), the material that demonstrates diagnostic Maltese cross birefringence under polarized light. Human patient tissue with clear EPP attribution from the case-report context. C: Polarized light microscopy of the liver biopsy (HE, 40×) showing red birefringence with the characteristic Maltese cross structure (white arrowheads) of protoporphyrin deposits — the pathognomonic histologic finding of...

(c) Polarized light microscopy shows red birefringence of the granular material, and the characteristic Maltese cross structure is visible (indicated by white arrowheads) (HE, 40×).

Infiltration of inflammatory cells is observed in the stroma, along with bile duct hyperplasia, mild hydropic degeneration, and mild fatty change in hepatocytes (Figure 2a). Dense brownish granular deposits were observed in the hepatic sinusoids and hepatocytes (Figure 2b). Under polarized light microscopy, the granular deposits exhibited red birefringence, with a characteristic Maltese cross pattern (Figure 2c). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Abdominal radiograph from an EPP case report showing intestinal obstruction/gas-liquid levels; in the article this presentation is attributed to protoporphyric neuropathy mimicking acute porphyria. Radiograph is a real patient image tied to the EPP diagnosis, but obstruction is a complication rather than a cardinal EPP sign. B: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT of the EPP patient showing hepatosplenomegaly while excluding biliary obstruction and tumors; supportive of EPP-related hepatopathy in this confirmed EPP case. C: Liver biopsy (HE x100) from the EPP case showing active cirrhosis and severe intrahepatic cholangitis, the histologic correlate of protoporphyric hepatopathy that caused acute liver failure. D: Clinical photograph of the dorsum of the hand showing leathery hyperkeratotic/waxy thickening over the knuckles with mild pitted scarring in light-exposed areas - the classic nonblistering phototoxic skin changes of EPP,...

(C) Liver biopsy indicated active cirrhosis and severe intrahepatic cholangitis (HE, ×100). (D) Nonblistering cutaneous photosensitivity in light-exposed areas.

The abdominal X-ray indicated multiple gas–liquid interface in the lower right abdomen (Figure 1A). Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly without evidence of biliary obstruction, tumors, or portal vascular abnormalities (Figure 1B). Liver biopsy indicated nodular hepatocellular hyperplasia and intrahepatic cholangitis (Figure 1C). Based on the patient’s clinical manifestations and history of photosensitivity (Figure 1D), porphyria remained a

agnosis. Painful nonblistering photosensitivity usually suggests the diagnosis of EPP, we suspected this potential based on further inquiry into the history of cutaneous photosensitivity. As shown in Figure 1D, it represents chronic changes of leathery hyperkeratotic skin and mild scarring especially in hands and finger joints. Patients with severe protoporphyric hepatopathy may develop a severe motor neuropathy similar to acute porphyrias, as characterized by abdominal pain, weakness, constipation, nausea and vomiting (5).
